points: Sports marketing: using sport to promote and sell products, services or places, and promoting sport itself to attract participants, spectators, sponsors and broadcasters.
Sports tourism: travel to take part in or watch sport, or to visit sporting attractions.
Active sports tourist: travels to take part, for example in golf, surfing, cycling, walking or running events.
Event sports tourist: travels to watch, for example international matches, golf tournaments or horse racing.
Nostalgia sports tourist: visits stadiums, museums and halls of fame.
Golf: Ireland is marketed as a destination for golf, so visitors travel specifically to play.
Surfing and water sports are marketed on the Wild Atlantic Way, a tourism route along Ireland's west coast.
Walking and cycling are marketed on greenways, which are off-road routes such as the Great Western Greenway in Co. Mayo and the Waterford Greenway.
Visitors who come specifically for an activity stay longer and spend more.

notes.h: Bidding for and hosting major international events
points: Bidding for and hosting major international events brings visiting teams, media and spectators to Ireland.
Hosting an event shows Ireland to a worldwide television audience.
The 2006 Ryder Cup was held at the K Club, Co. Kildare; the 2027 Ryder Cup is scheduled for Adare Manor, Co. Limerick.
The Tour de France began in Dublin in 1998.
Six Nations matches are played at the Aviva Stadium, Dublin.
American college football games have been played at the Aviva Stadium, Dublin.
Annual events attract visitors every year, such as the Galway Races, an annual horse-racing festival in Galway.
The Irish Open, a professional golf championship held in Ireland, attracts visitors every year.
Spectacle events in scenic locations market the landscape: the Red Bull Cliff Diving World Series has held events on Inis Mór in the Aran Islands.
Sporting heritage attractions: the GAA Museum and stadium tours at Croke Park, Dublin.
Famous athletes and teams are used in tourism campaigns to publicise Ireland.

notes.h: Evaluating the potential of sports marketing for tourism in Ireland
points: High potential for activity tourism, given Ireland's landscape and Irish sporting culture.
Heritage tourism also has high potential, rooted in Irish sporting culture.
The potential depends on investment in facilities and transport.
The benefits depend on being spread locally, beyond the venue and the event weekend.

questions.prompt: Discuss the potential of sports marketing for the development of tourism in Ireland.
questions.model: Sports marketing can develop Ireland's tourism in four ways. First, Ireland is marketed for specific activities: golf, surfing and water sports on the Wild Atlantic Way, a tourism route along the west coast, and walking and cycling on greenways such as the Great Western Greenway in Co. Mayo. Visitors who come for an activity stay longer and spend more. Second, hosting major international events brings visiting teams, media and spectators, and shows Ireland to a worldwide television audience. Examples are the 2006 Ryder Cup at the K Club in Co. Kildare, the Six Nations matches and American college football games at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, and the Tour de France start in Dublin in 1998. The 2027 Ryder Cup is scheduled for Adare Manor in Co. Limerick. Third, annual events attract visitors every year, such as the Galway Races and the Irish Open golf championship. Fourth, spectacle and heritage marketing uses scenic places and sporting history: the Red Bull Cliff Diving World Series has held events on Inis Mór, and the GAA Museum and stadium tours at Croke Park draw visitors interested in sporting heritage. The benefits are economic, through spending on accommodation, food, transport and retail, jobs, taxes, and benefits spread to rural and coastal areas; they also include a positive international image, facilities that remain for local people, and community pride, volunteering and participation. The limitations are the public cost of bidding, hosting and security, money leaving the area through international companies, congestion and rising prices for residents, environmental damage, facilities that are under-used after an event, and Ireland's weather, limited large venues and transport links. Overall, the potential is high for activity and heritage tourism, given Ireland's landscape and sporting culture, but it depends on investment in facilities and transport and on spreading the benefits beyond the event itself.

questions.prompt: Explain sports marketing and describe one way it could help develop tourism in Ireland.
questions.model: Sports marketing means using sport to promote and sell products, services or places, and promoting sport itself to attract participants, spectators, sponsors and broadcasters. One way it could develop tourism in Ireland is by marketing the country as a destination for golf. Visitors travel specifically to play on Irish courses, stay longer and spend more, which brings income to hotels, restaurants and transport operators. The Irish Open golf championship, held in Ireland each year, adds to this by attracting visitors for the event itself.
